title: The fifth start is stopped cleanly and kept; a test of a pi oracle runs on the five cards
text: On the owner's word ("restart the cluster with the pie oracle test") all seven nodes were asked to store their regions and stop between 13:28:43 and 13:34:55 UTC. Every node stopped cleanly; the data stays where it is and the start can go on from these rounds. Since 13:38 UTC (rig B) and 13:41 UTC (rig A) the five graphics cards run a test that is not part of this start: rules 8 with an oracle that reads the decimal digits of pi off the bytes of each program and gives a stretch of land less light the further it is behind its region's best. Each card is a world of its own with its own setting, one of them without the oracle as the control. The processors compute no world in the test. Nothing of the test is on the tracker's pages.

title: All seven bands run again, with a night that comes from the machine
text: From 11:11 to 11:19 UTC all seven nodes were stopped cleanly, given new code and started again; rig B's three card nodes went on from the rounds at which their guards had stopped them the evening before. New with this code is a night by rest, the user's idea of this morning: if the cards heat up they are cooled down, with less energy, and this shows as night. A node now looks at its machine after every round, taking the hottest reading since its last look. On rig B night falls on its bands when any of its graphics cards has been at 77 degrees, or when the kernel counts a single new bus error. A node at night waits after each round, so that its device works a fifth of the time; its meter reads on, and since under rules 7 a band's light is what its device draws, the band gets about a quarter of its daylight. Day breaks at the look after a rest, five minutes at the earliest, when the machine has cooled. Rig A's limits are far above where it runs, so it has no night. The limits are settings of the machines, no rule of the world, and the rules' fingerprint is unchanged. Two rehearsals on rig B's three cards came first (no bus error in 58 minutes at or near full power), and two reviews, which found among other things that a look at one moment misses the heat (a card is eight degrees cooler seconds after its work) and that a stuck reading of a card could have left a node hanging. The first night of the running world fell at 11:19:50 UTC, four minutes after the start: the processor's band and two of the three card bands of rig B went dark within 25 seconds of each other, and the processor cooled from 64 to 35 degrees in three minutes. What a night does to a band was measured at once: under a quarter of its light, more than half of its organisms starve in the first night round (6.28 million to 2.68 million in the band of the hottest card), and in the rehearsal a band was back at nine tenths of its number three day rounds after dawn. The guard beside each node has a third case as well: if the kernel counts bus errors fast, it stops a card's node cleanly while the machine can still be reached.

title: Four of the seven bands run again; rig B's three cards wait for a guardrail
text: At 08:53 UTC the three nodes of rig A and the processor's node of rig B were started again. Each went on from the round at which its guard had stopped it the evening before; nothing had been lost. The three card nodes of rig B stay stopped for now. Both times rig B lost the link to its chipset, its three cards and its processor had run at full power for a while, its lowest card at 81 to 84 degrees with its fan at its limit, and the kernel had counted bus errors by the thousand in the minutes before. With the cards off, its processor's node runs at 54 degrees and the kernel counts no error. So the cards come back when two things are in place: a node that rests its device when the machine runs too hot, which under rules 7 makes its band dark (the user's idea: a night that comes from the real machine), and a guard that stops the card nodes on the first fast run of bus errors, while the machine can still be reached. Both are built and are being rehearsed on rig B's cards beside the running world.

title: Why both rigs went off the network: rig A's network chip lost its link, rig B lost everything behind its chipset a second time
text: Both machines were switched off and on at 08:33 UTC on 13 November and answered again from 08:37. Their kernel logs give two different causes. On rig A, at 17:33:25 UTC, the network chip dropped off its own PCI Express link and the kernel detached it. The 4090 behind the same chipset, the drive and everything else worked on, and the machine logged no bus error at all. Link power saving is switched on for that chip. On rig B the course of 13:50:59 UTC repeated itself at 16:50:09: correctable bus errors on every device behind the chipset and on the link between processor and chipset, rising from a few lines a minute to 2,600 a minute within 20 to 50 minutes, then a fatal error the kernel could not recover from, and everything behind the chipset gone until the power was cycled. There was not one such line in the six days before 12 November. Both times the three cards and the processor had run at full power for 18 to 40 minutes, the third card at 83 to 84 degrees with its fan at 99%. Link power saving is off on every link of rig B, so that is not the cause there; heat is the leading explanation and is not proven. Rig B's three card nodes stay stopped until their guard can stop them on the first bus errors, before the link fails.

title: Rig A went off the network; its guards stopped its three nodes cleanly at 17:43 UTC, and the fifth start stood still
text: Rig A stopped answering at 17:33 UTC, 43 minutes after rig B. Its readings went on every minute as well. By them its network port stayed up, but passed its last bytes between 17:33:00 and 17:34:00 and not one after that, in either direction, until the machine was switched off and on the next morning. Its guards found at 17:33:43 that nothing answered and stopped its three nodes cleanly at 17:43 UTC: the processor's at round 241, the 4090's at round 287 and the 4080's at round 277, with 57.8 million organisms in 138,194 inhabited regions. With that every node of the fifth start was stopped, each cleanly and by its guard, 95 minutes after the start. The world stood still with 87.4 million organisms in 223,883 inhabited regions until four of its nodes were started again at 08:53 UTC on 13 November.

title: Rig B went off the network again; its guards stopped its four nodes cleanly at 17:00 UTC
text: Rig B stopped answering at 16:50 UTC, 1 h 54 min after it had been switched on again. The machine itself ran on, and its own readings went on every minute: its network port was up at 16:50:00 and no port was up from 16:51:00 until the machine was switched off and on the next morning. Its four guards found at 16:50:14 that nothing answered, waited their ten minutes and stopped its four nodes cleanly at 17:00 UTC: the processor's at round 322, the three cards' at rounds 183, 177 and 179, with 29.6 million organisms in 85,689 inhabited regions between them. From 16:52 UTC on nothing arrived at any of the four any more, not even from each other, and by 17:00 the travellers waiting for a link had risen from about 8,000 to 122,000; every link was still called up. Rig A's three nodes ran on and called their links to rig B down within twenty minutes.

title: The fifth start began under rules 7: seven devices in a ring
text: Every processor and every graphics card of the two machines is now a world of its own: seven bands of land in a ring, 286,720 regions in all, each with its own founder. The light of a band is the electricity its device really draws, read every round, so the world starts in twilight and brightens as it fills. After 70 seconds: 18,727 inhabited regions, 5.0 million organisms, 725 of 1,056 watts, every link between the seven up. Before the start the engines, all five cards and the scripts that run the world were checked, and all seven nodes were started, stopped and resumed once on test data. Each node has a guard that stops it cleanly if its machine runs out of memory or loses its network.

title: Why rig B went off the network: its mainboard lost the link to its chipset
text: Rig B is back since 14:55 UTC, after being switched off and on. Its kernel log gives the cause: at 13:50:59 UTC the mainboard lost the link to its chipset, a PCI Express error that the kernel could not recover. Both network ports, the wireless card, USB and SATA are behind the chipset and went with it. The processor, the memory, the three graphics cards and the drive are not, and kept working. So rig B's node ran on without a network for an hour, to round 348 with 175,574 inhabited regions and 63.9 million organisms, and nobody could reach it to stop it cleanly. What was in its memory at the switch-off is gone; its drive holds its regions as of round 167. There was no bus error in the six days before and none since the restart. The earlier entry said its last reading was at round 293: that was the last one the tracker could fetch. To do: a guard on each rig that stops the node cleanly when the network has been gone for some minutes.

title: Rig B went off the network; the fourth start ended at round 1,705 on rig A
text: Rig B stopped answering between 13:47 and 13:50 UTC. Its last reading shows nothing that explains it: 48 GB of RAM free, no memory pressure, the CPU at 67 degrees, the three cards at 57, 67 and 80 degrees. It needs a look at the machine itself. Rig A noticed at its round 1,671, kept the travellers for rig B waiting, turned them back after ten minutes, and ran on alone for 34 rounds. On the owner's word it was stopped cleanly at 14:37 UTC at round 1,705, with 183,559 inhabited regions and 72.6 million organisms. Rig B's last known state is round 293 with 127,222 regions and 52.3 million organisms. The last status and map of both are kept in archive/sun-4 with a table. The next start is planned under rules 7 on rig A alone.

title: Rules 6 run: the fourth start began at 12:10 UTC from the two founders, the third start is kept
text:
The owner ordered rules 6 to be started as the fourth start as soon as their checks passed. The third start, under rules 5, was stopped cleanly for it: rig B wrote its last status at 12:02 UTC at round 252, rig A at 12:03 UTC at round 330. It had run for 93 minutes and held 84.3 million organisms on 258,149 regions. Its data is kept under the tag sun-v3.

Both nodes started again at 12:10 UTC from the two founders, a plant on rig A and a grazer on rig B, on commit fb7f53a.

Rules 6 in short: energy comes only from light and from eating, the tasks are gone, and every sense and every act costs energy. Twelve senses sit behind the instruction `in` and five acts behind `out`: rest, give, graze, mark and name. Every organism shows a word that it inherits from its mother and can call out.

At 12:20 UTC, ten minutes after the start, rig B stood at round 133 with 18,623 inhabited regions and 7.2 million organisms. Rig A's plant clan had not left its first region: 483 organisms at round 1,014.

Source: each node's status at the end of a round, as the samplers on the rigs recorded it.

title: The sun-4 start began under the new rules
The sun-3 start stopped cleanly and kept
First results of rules 5: guard, sense and feel appeared by mutation, bites are parried, the clans have met
text:
No founder can guard, sense or feel under rules 5: the three instructions have to appear by mutation. They did in the first minute. Rig A's status at round 1 counted no organism with any of them, and at round 6, at 10:31 UTC, the first with each.

At 11:14 UTC, 43 minutes after the start, rig A stood at round 267 with 104,185 inhabited regions and 32.2 million organisms. Of them 4.2 million could guard, 1.9 million sense and 0.5 million feel. 725,337 bites were parried in that round and 21.9 million since the start. Rig B stood at round 193 with 66,080 regions and 21.8 million organisms. Together the rigs ran 2.8 billion instructions per second.

At 11:56 UTC rig A stood at round 326 with 149,055 regions and 54.8 million organisms: 7.4 million could guard (13.5%), 3.8 million sense (7.0%) and 0.8 million feel (1.4%). 1,946,815 bites were parried in that round, 21.3% of the bites that reached a living body, and 65.1 million since the start. At 11:58 UTC rig B stood at round 247 with 102,134 regions and 25.5 million organisms: 1.1 million could guard (4.2%), 1.3 million sense (5.2%) and 0.2 million feel (1.0%). 81,350 bites were parried in that round, 1.6% of those that reached a living body, and 9.7 million since the start. Together the rigs ran 2.1 billion instructions per second.

The clans have met. The first 506 organisms of rig A's clan were counted on rig B at 10:36 UTC, at rig B's round 75, within six minutes of the start. At 11:14 UTC 3.3 million of them lived on rig B and at 11:58 UTC 4.1 million, 16.0% of rig B's organisms. None of rig B's clan lived on rig A.

Source: each node's status at the end of a round, as the samplers on the rigs recorded it.

title: Higher write budgets for the drives: 500 GB a day on rig A, 120 on rig B (204d4e7)
text:
The user chose to raise the budgets that limit how much the nodes write to their drives a day: from 100 to 500 GB on rig A and from 30 to 120 GB on rig B. Rig A also gets 8aa1f73, which moves the memory allocator's threshold to 16 KB. A clean stop and start of both rigs in parallel, on the same run and the same files, with 20 to 25 minutes down expected. From this start on, a budget can be changed without a restart: the node rereads its configuration when it is signalled.

How it went: rig A finished round 561 at 09:02 UTC, writing at 118 GB a day against its old budget of 100, and rig B round 585 at 08:58; both had stopped cleanly by 09:04 and started at 09:04:57. Rig A finished round 562 at 09:12 and rig B round 586 at 09:15, so no round was lost; rig A was out of rounds for 11 minutes and rig B for 17. The stall alarm raised nothing.

title: Rig B: the memory allocator's threshold at 16 KB and a smaller ready tier per worker (8aa1f73)
text: A clean stop of rig B after round 583 and a start at 08:36:19 UTC, on the same run and the same files; rig A ran on. With the allocator's threshold at 16 KB and a ready tier of 800 MB per worker, a worker's heap came to 283 MB instead of 1,344 MB, the CPU workers held 37.1 GB for 31.2 GB of data, and 15.8 GB of memory stayed free outside the dawn (8.7 GB before). Its deflated tier is full, so rig B now pages about 8 GB a day of its 30 GB budget, without waiting. Both rigs' worlds no longer fit in their memory. The stall alarm raised nothing: the stop and the start fell between two readings, and the clean stop reset its clock.

A clean stop and start of both rigs, on the same run and the same files. The workers give memory they no longer need back to the machine, and the workers that drive the cards delete their round files from shared memory. With rounds of 9 to 11 minutes, about 180 and 195 million organisms on rig A and rig B, the stop waits for the current round and the store, and the first round after the start reloads every region: 20 to 30 minutes down were expected. How it went: rig A finished round 556 at 08:03 UTC and had stopped cleanly by 08:07; rig B finished round 581 at 08:06 and stopped between two readings. Both nodes started at 08:10:09 and finished their first rounds at 08:21, rig B round 582 and rig A round 557, each in about 11 minutes, so no round was lost and the rigs were out of rounds for about 15 to 18 minutes. The stall alarm raised nothing.

title: Travellers deflated and let go after sending; both nodes started again (6937102)
text: The cause of both crashes: since 9044974 the batches of travellers were the engine's records, not deflated. At dawn one round's travellers came to about 10 GB on rig A, and the node's main process held them two to three times over. The fix: the workers deflate the batches (5.1 times smaller, measured), and the main process lets go of its copy of the arrivals as soon as they are sent. The cards get a 384 KB arena for leavers, because the dawn give-backs (up to 13,730 regions in a round on one card) all came from the 128 KB arena running full; their slots are reduced to fit, to 57,000 and 25,000 regions on rig A and 25,000 on each of rig B's three cards. Checked with the world's tests, the link journal's checks and the node check on the RTX 4090 with the new arena. Both rigs' workers stored every region when their main processes died (all 283,527 of rig B's region files were rewritten), so the start reads them all first, as after any unclean stop, and then goes on: little or nothing of the world is lost. RUNTIME watches both rigs through the next dawn.

title: rig B: the node is not running, and did not stop cleanly
text: Its process was gone at 21:54 UTC, and its running file is still there. Its last round, 478, ended at 21:52 UTC.

title: Rig B's node killed by the kernel for lack of memory, after round 478
text: At 21:52 UTC rig B had 1 GB of its 62 GB of memory available. Its node's main process held 11.3 GB, with travellers piling up for the neighbour on rig A, which had been down since 21:38 UTC. RUNTIME's session was not running, so COORD sent the normal clean stop at 21:52:33 UTC. Round 478 finished (282,421 regions, 112.7 million organisms). Then the kernel's out-of-memory killer stopped the main process at 21:52:55 UTC, with 18.7 GB resident, before the store began. The node's running file was left behind, so this was an unclean stop; the store that the stop request started may have hastened it. Both rigs come back from their last stored files when RUNTIME decides; nothing is restarted until then.

title: rig A: no new round for 14 minutes
text: The node is not running, and it did not stop cleanly: its last round, 448, ended at 21:37 UTC. Its usual round takes 3.4 minutes (the median of its last 10, or the last if that took longer), and the alarm stands at 3 times that.

title: Rig A's node killed by the kernel for lack of memory, after round 448
text: The kernel's out-of-memory killer stopped rig A's node at 21:38:05 UTC, nine seconds after round 448 ended, with 19.2 GB resident. It was not a clean stop: the node's running file was left behind, and its other processes ended over the next five minutes. In the five rounds before, rig A's organisms rose from 58.2 million (round 443) to 66.4, 82.0, 94.8, 101.7 and 105.0 million, while the dead bodies fell from 71 million to 9.8 million; free memory on the machine was down to between 0.9 and 1.7 GB of 62 GB. Rig B ran on until 21:52 UTC, when it was killed the same way (its own entry). The stall alarm raised it at 21:52 UTC, and it was passed on to the session that watches the rigs.

title: The cards hold regions as packed bytes (208e47f)
text: Clean stops at 19:01 UTC (rig A, after round 354) and 19:03 UTC (rig B, after round 381). A hard-link copy of each node's data folder was taken first; both nodes started again at 19:04 UTC, on the same run and the same files. Both were back in rounds by 19:07 UTC: rig B finished round 382 at 19:06:33 UTC, 137 seconds after its start, and rig A round 355 at 19:06:55 UTC, after 161 seconds. The stall alarm raised nothing. The cards now hold their regions as packed bytes (the merge of cards-packed): about 64,000 and 34,000 regions per card on rig A and about 29,000 on each of three cards on rig B, with a slow first round while the cards are filled. Per card, the status gains keptOnItsCpu, launchSeconds and givenBack (paused in passes, in arrivals, too large for its slot); since 00d7c79 it also has cardWorkerTimePercent beside workerTimePercent. If the first rounds go wrong, the plan is to go back to 1bfb123 before 19:45 UTC.

title: CPU workers keep regions as packed bytes and run whole rounds in C
text:
Clean stop from 16:30:54 to 16:42:10 UTC (the old workers on rig B took 11 minutes to store), start at 16:42:17
UTC, no errors and no damaged files since. Region files become packed bytes, deflated; every region file was
converted during the first round after the start. A hard-link copy of each node's data was made beside it before
the start, as a way back.

Second round after the start: rig A did round 262 in 89 seconds at 1,000 million instructions per second, with
57,354 regions ready as packed bytes in 11.0 GB of RAM; rig B did round 288 in 107 seconds at 972 million per
second, with 62,452 regions in 11.8 GB. The workers now spend about 90% of their time running the world; turning
travellers into text and back, which took a tenth to a quarter of it before, is gone.

title: Tracking started - one reading a minute of each rig and of the world on it
text:
A sampler on each rig records the node's status, the CPUs, memory, drives, temperatures and the graphics cards
once a minute, and keeps a copy of the map every 30 minutes. Before this the history of the runs comes from the
nodes' logs, one line a minute with the round but without the time.

title: Regions that do not fit are kept as file bytes in RAM instead of being paged to the SSD
text:
Clean stop at 15:59:35 UTC and start at 16:04:19 UTC. Right after it rig A did a round in 36 seconds with no wait
for the disk budget: 24,000 regions held as objects and 19,322 as file bytes in 734 MB of RAM. Before, rig A
computed for about 30 seconds per round and then waited about 3 minutes for the budget, rig B 2 minutes and then
5 to 6 minutes.

title: No limit on land - the memory and disk use of the world are to be optimised instead
text:
The world grows by more than a thousand regions a minute and had reached what the two rigs hold in video memory
and RAM. Beyond that, regions were paged to the SSDs under a write budget and the rigs waited minutes per round.
Of the three ways out (a limit on land, larger write budgets, tighter memory) the choice was tighter memory.

title: Restart - fewer regions in the CPU workers' RAM, so the card workers have room
text: Clean stop at 15:28 UTC and start at 15:30 UTC.

title: The clans have met again, one-sided as in the first world; half of all organisms starve each night
text:
1.8 million organisms of the clan from rig A lived on rig B, and none of the other clan on rig A. Populations swing
with day and night: more than half of all organisms starve every night. Rig A, from a plant only: 84% plants only,
16% plants that also eat. Rig B, from a grazer: 55% and 45%.

title: Restart - travellers go to and from a card in pieces, with no ceiling on their total
text: Clean stop at 15:15 UTC and start at 15:18 UTC.

title: Restart - the census after an unclean stop keeps no regions in memory
text: Clean stop at 14:45 UTC and start at 14:47 UTC.

title: Started again - both nodes rebuilt their state from the region files
text:
Regions now go to a card 256 at a time. Rig A read 49,196 region files and went on from clock 170, rig B read
45,755 and went on from clock 191. No traveller on the road was lost.

title: The card workers ran out of memory on both rigs and both nodes went down
text:
Each card worker loaded every region it was given into its own memory at once. The nodes stopped without storing,
so the regions held in memory fell back to their last stored state.

title: The five graphics cards join - regions kept in video memory between rounds
text:
Clean stop at 14:32 UTC and start at 14:34 UTC. The same C source runs on the cards, one GPU thread per region,
with the same bytes as on a CPU.

title: Regions now computed by C compiled to WebAssembly, about six times as fast
text:
Clean stop at 13:38 UTC and start at 13:39 UTC. The C engine gives the same bytes as the JavaScript definition of
the rules, checked region by region. The cluster went from about 100 million to about 890 million instructions per
second.

title: The sun world started again from the founders, under corrected rules and with old age
text:
The four rule defects are fixed and bodies now wear out: an organism dies after spending 200,000 flips. Removing
the hidden subsidy of debt made breeding harder for poor mothers, which was tested on single regions and small
worlds before this start.

title: The sun world stopped - a review confirmed 19 defects, 4 in the rules
text:
Energy could be made from nothing by eating cheap children, reserves could go below zero, `look` counted dead
bodies, and rounds could stretch until time stood still in a region. Run kept at tag `sun-v1`. At the stop rig A
held 12.7 million organisms, 94% of them plants only; rig B 6.0 million, 73% of them plants that also eat.

title: The sun world started - light, stored energy, eating, the dead
text:
Energy now enters only as light and every instruction is paid from a reserve. Rig A starts from a plant, rig B
from a grazer, a plant that eats once in its life.

title: The first world stopped cleanly and kept
text:
Final state: 40.7 million organisms in 89,672 inhabited regions. Rig A at round 174 with 22.8 million organisms,
rig B at round 148 with 17.9 million, of them 620,680 from the clan of rig A. Code at tag `world-v1`; the data is
kept and the run can be resumed.

title: First contact between the two clans, and it is one-sided
text:
About 17 hours after the start the clans had met: 565,000 organisms of the clan from rig A lived on rig B, and not
one of the clan from rig B lived on rig A. The faster rig's clan reached the border first and settled the empty
land beyond it. An arrival leaves about half as many descendants as a resident, so whoever settles first keeps the
land. At the contact line the clan from rig A advanced east by about a quarter of a column per round.

title: The first world started on both rigs
text:
One plain ancestor per rig, 100 columns from the shared border. Every inhabited region runs a fixed 1,000,000
instructions per round. A first attempt was restarted from the founders after a few dozen rounds; the run that
counts began with that restart.
